# Quality improvements

@difference Extension: a reversed 32-bit float depth buffer, up to 127 lights per scene, surfaces with more than 65535 vertices and trilinear mip maps, all without any change to the program.

Things that look better or no longer break compared to the originals, with no change to your program.

## Depth buffer

The depth buffer is reversed and a 32-bit float: the near plane of `CameraRange` is written as 1 and the far plane as 0, and the closer surface wins. Blitz3D used a 16 or 24-bit buffer that is 0 at the near plane, which spends most of its precision close to the camera and makes far surfaces flicker through each other (z-fighting). With the reversed float buffer the precision is almost even over the whole range, so distant surfaces that are close together stay apart without having to push `near` out. This changes nothing a program can see except that z-fighting is much rarer. The depth is still not linear in the buffer itself (it is `near / distance` for a perspective camera, and linear for `CameraProjMode 2`), but the buffer is never read back by a program: `ProjectedZ` is the distance in front of the camera, and `Graphics3D`'s depth argument is not used.

## Many lights

Blitz3D uses the fixed function lights of Direct3D 7, which are limited to eight for the whole scene: the lights after the eighth do nothing. BlitzLLVM keeps up to 127 visible lights per camera and gives every draw its own set of eight, chosen on the CPU when the draw is made. A light is rated by its brightness (the color of `LightColor`) times its attenuation (range over distance) at the closest point of the sphere around the entity's box, which is the most it can do anywhere on the entity, and the eight with the highest rating are used. Negative lights, which darken, are rated by the size of their color, so a strong one is not left out for a weak positive one. Lights that do almost nothing there (the rating is below 1/512) are left out, and directional lights are rated by their color alone.

With [EntityLightChannel](EntityLightChannel) only the lights that share a channel with an entity are rated for it, so lights of other channels never use up one of its eight. Planes, terrains and fullbright entities take the first eight of the lights that share a channel with them.

A scene with eight lights or fewer is lit exactly as before, and a program written for the original behaves the same unless it has more than eight visible lights. Entities without a box (planes and terrains) and fullbright entities are not rated: planes and terrains use the first eight lights. Spot cones are not taken into account in the rating. The lights are not part of the batching: draws that are the same in everything else still merge into one call, as each instance carries its own set of lights. Order and blending of see-through things are not changed.

## Large meshes

A surface made with [CreateSurface](CreateSurface), [AddVertex](AddVertex) and [AddTriangle](AddTriangle) can hold more than 65535 vertices, and a triangle can use any of them. The original Blitz3D and Blitz3D_Soloud keep triangle corners as 16 bit numbers, so a surface with more vertices crashes in `RenderWorld`. Here the corners are 32 bit numbers, so `CountVertices` and `CountTriangles` count everything you added and every triangle is drawn.

![A grid of 78000 vertices, red up to vertex 65535 and blue after it](media/meshes/large-mesh.png)

## Mip maps

Textures with flag 8 get a chain of mip maps and are sampled with trilinear filtering, which blends between two levels. The levels are made by averaging 2 by 2 texels, so masked (flag 4) and alpha textures average their alpha as well, which is also what the original did and makes their edges soft from afar. The levels of a texture that is drawn on (`TextureBuffer`) are made again before the texture is next used in a scene. The levels that are stored in a block compressed DDS file are used instead of made ones. The frames of a texture (`LoadAnimTexture`, `CreateTexture` with frames) are the layers of one image and each has levels of its own, so the levels never blend frames (only a block compressed or deep picture loaded with `LoadAnimTexture` stays a sheet, and then they do). Flag 8 alone does not use anisotropic filtering, but a texture can be given it with a sampler ([CreateSampler](CreateSampler), [SetSamplerAnisotropy](SetSamplerAnisotropy) and [SetTextureSampler](SetTextureSampler)), which the originals had no way to do:

```blitzbasic
tex = LoadTexture("floor.png", 1 + 8)
sampler = CreateSampler()
SetSamplerAnisotropy sampler, 8
SetTextureSampler tex, sampler
```

See [CreateSampler](CreateSampler) for the rest of the settings.
